planting.note: Install container-grown or bare-root plants in early spring on a rocky slope, bluff, or streambank site with sharp drainage, since this species naturally roots into shallow, gravelly soil pockets.

directions: Hairy mock orange is a compact deciduous shrub of rocky bluffs, river gorges, and moist ledges scattered through the central and southern Appalachians, distinguished from the more widespread Philadelphus inodorus by its fragrant, four-petaled white flowers and softly hairy young stems and leaf undersides. Clusters of sweetly scented blooms open in late spring and draw bumblebees, mason bees, and other early-summer pollinators to woodland edges where few other shrubs are yet flowering. It performs best on a lean, well-drained, slightly rocky slope with morning sun and afternoon shade, mimicking the cliff and ravine habitats where it grows wild. Renewal-prune the oldest canes to the ground every few years after flowering to keep the multi-stemmed form vigorous and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated stock in early spring along a streambank or seasonally scoured floodplain edge in consistently moist, gravelly to sandy soil, since wild populations depend on periodic flood disturbance to persist.

directions: Virginia spiraea is a federally threatened, rhizomatous shrub restricted to a scatter of high-gradient river and stream banks in the central Appalachians, where its dense root mats stabilize scoured cobble bars against flood erosion. In cultivation it forms a low, arching, suckering thicket topped in early to midsummer by flat-topped clusters of small white to pale pink flowers that draw a wide range of native bees and butterflies. Because the species is adapted to periodic flooding and mechanical scouring, it tolerates seasonally saturated soil and occasional inundation far better than most garden spireas, but it should never be collected from the wild given its rarity. Site it along a pond margin, rain garden, or streambank restoration planting with reliable moisture and light shade for part of the day.
sources: Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation Natural Heritage Program
